title: [2506.04290] Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy

sections.heading: Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy

content.text: Large Language Models (LLM), which have developed in recent years, enable credit risk assessment through the analysis of financial texts such as analyst reports and corporate disclosures. This paper presents the first systematic review and taxonomy focusing on LLM-based approaches in credit risk estimation. We determined the basic model architectures by selecting 60 relevant papers published between 2020-2025 with the PRISMA research strategy. And we examined the data used for scenarios such as credit default prediction and risk analysis. Since the main focus of the paper is interpretability, we classify concepts such as explainability mechanisms, chain of thought prompts and natural language justifications for LLM-based credit models.

The taxonomy organizes the literature under four main headings: model architectures, data types, explainability mechanisms and application areas. Based on this analysis, we highlight the main future trends and research gaps for LLM-based credit scoring systems. This paper aims to be a reference paper for artificial intelligence and financial researchers.
This manuscript remains under review.

Credit risk assessment is one of the important components in financial decision making, such as making investment decisions and determining whether to grant credit to an individual or institution [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib1)]. While traditional methods rely on structured data such as financial ratios and past payment information when assessing credit risk, in reality important information about the credit may not be available in an organized manner [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib2)]. An example of this is that executive comments, economic news and analyst reports are generally in free text (unstructured).

Advanced LLM models such as GPT and FinBERT have great potential in financial applications with their high performance in extracting meaning from free text [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib3), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib4)]. They can produce interpretable outputs by making sense of complex financial data and thus facilitate decision-making processes [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib5)]. With its high potential, this research area, LLM-Driven Credit Risk Assessment, where Natural Language Processing (NLP), financial analysis and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) intersect, has begun to attract the attention of researchers. However, the applications of LLMs in the field of credit risk analysis have not yet been systematically examined. The majority of studies in the literature superficially examine the applications of artificial intelligence in the financial sector or do not address the interpretability of LLMs in credit risk assessment in detail. Moreover, this particular research area requires a comprehensive taxonomy of LLM model types, data sources and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques.
This paper systematically reviews LLM-based approaches in credit risk assessment and presents a detailed taxonomy study. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

* • Published studies for LLM-based credit risk applications are systematically reviewed with the PRISMA methodology. * • A detailed taxonomy is presented by examining the current research from four main aspects: model architecture, data modality, explainability mechanism and application area. * • Trends, challenges and open research directions in the deployment of LLMs are analyzed. * • The first systematic review and taxonomy focusing on LLM-based approaches in credit risk estimation is presented, providing a reference for researchers and financial institutions in the field.

Although there has been increasing interest in LLM and artificial intelligence (AI)-based financial studies in recent years, there is still no comprehensive classification in terms of focus, depth and relevance to credit risk, and discussions about interpretability, a key component in credit assessment scenarios, are lacking.

Staegemann et al. [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib6)], in their literature review on generative AI applications in banking, highlight the potential of LLMs for risk reduction and customer experience. However, the article does not include techniques for credit risk modeling or interpretability, and there is no taxonomy of model types. In [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib7)], models such as FinGPT and BloombergGPT are discussed, LLMs address financial inclusion and policy implications, and ethical concerns, but ignore credit risk applications. In Joshi et al. study’s AI frameworks in credit risk and trading applications are examined, but does not include LLM architectures or datasets. [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib8)]. Chen et al. [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib9)], in their study of LLMs in finance, law, and healthcare, also highlight the risks of using LLMs in high-risk sectors. However, the financial discussion is superficial, and credit scoring methods are not addressed. In [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib10)], sentiment analysis techniques used in banking are reviewed, and the focus is on examining the impact on investor confidence. However, credit risk tasks are only superficially examined. In Nie et al. study’s the research on generative AI and LLMs focused on risk modeling and deployment architectures [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib11)]. The paper discusses areas such as data engineering, credit scoring modules, etc. but lacks a comparative taxonomy and interpretability mechanisms for LLM types. Zavitsanos et al. [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib12)] examines ML approaches in financial risk detection, examining features, data labels, evaluation techniques, and ML methods. Although this is a useful taxonomy, it is more focused on ML than LLM. In [[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib13)], the authors mainly emphasize traditional ML and statistical-based methods for financial forecasting, but do not address large language models or explainable AI methods. In Joshi et al. study’s research on AI frameworks in credit risk and trading applications, but does not focus on LLM-specific taxonomy or performance benchmarking [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib14)]. Kong et al. [[15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib15)] presented a study that benchmarked LLM-based financial tasks for three different languages (Chinese, Japanese, English). However, the model types are not classified and also the explainability is not analyzed for credit risk domains. In Joshi et al. study’s [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib16)]. provides detailed architectural review on LLM-based applications for credit scoring and macroeconomic simulations. However, the paper lacks empirical comparison and also lacks a classification for interpretability. Lee et al. [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib17)] review domain-specific financial applications based on LLM, but categorizes flow tasks and datasets, but does not focus on credit risk subdomains. In [[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib18)] investigates AI-based methods in financial scenarios such as fraud detection and portfolio management, but does not provide a detailed review of model interpretability and LLM for credit scoring. In Karami and Igbokwe study examines AI-based risk assessment and limitations of traditional credit methods, but does not provide a classification of LLM [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib19)]. Alonso et al. [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib20)] provides an overview of LLMs in areas such as asset management and risk reporting, but is insufficient for credit risk. In [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib21)], LLMs are studied for financial applications such as credit analysis and fraud detection. However, they are very superficial in interpretability and credit-specific modeling. Lakkaraju et al. [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib22)] evaluates LLM performance through a fairness lens, focuses on bias reduction strategies such as improving user trust, but credit risk assessments and explainability are very superficial. In [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib23)], LLM-based financial sentiment analysis with multiple datasets is not considered credit risk or XAI. Omoseebi et al. [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib24)] investigates the financial security side of LLMs such as fraud detection, but does not perform detailed credit risk modeling and taxonomy studies. In [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib25)], democratization of financial datasets and open data models of LLMs are discussed, but no empirical comparison is included for credit or risk analytics. Krause et al. [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib26)] present a survey discussing the sustainability of LLM models such as ChatGPT. The survey is mostly on ethical and governance concerns and is superficial in terms of credit scoring, model breakdowns, and datasets. In [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib27)], the robustness of LLMs in financial tasks is assessed and benchmarks are made on summarization and event detection. However, the study does not include credit-related tasks and explainability is weak.

Comparison of Surveys: Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Surveys ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") provides a comparison of the surveys examined in this section. While interest in the financial domain applications of LLMs is increasing day by day, existing studies focus on broad themes such as generative AI [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib6)], inclusiveness frameworks [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib7)] and financial NLP [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib17), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib21)]. Only a limited number of studies directly focus on credit risk tasks, and none of them provide a taxonomy by examining LLM architectures, data formats, interpretability techniques and domain-specific applications.

Furthermore, most studies do not provide interpretability for high-risk decisions such as credit scoring, and the studies that do provide interpretability are very superficial [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib20), [25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib25)]. Some of the surveys include studies such as sentiment analysis or fraud detection [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib23), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib10)], but they do not address the concept of credit risk modeling. Some of the reviewed studies focus only on traditional machine learning (ML) [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib12), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib19)] and only propose conceptual frameworks without model comparison [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib8), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib16)].

Although some of the studies discuss domain-specific LLMs (such as FinBERT, FinGPT, and InvestLM), they do not systematically model architecture or risk. None of the existing studies provide a classification of LLM applications that addresses both modeling and regulatory requirements (e.g., explainability, data provenance, or fairness). This study is the first to fill this gap based on four main pillars: model architecture, data modality, interpretability mechanism, and application domain.
This section describes the methodology used in the systematic review of LLM-based credit risk assessment.

For the paper collection, refereed journals, high-ranking conferences, book chapters covering the years 2020-2025 were collected by scanning libraries such as IEEE Xplore, Elsevier, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, Scopus and arXiv. The following keywords were used while scanning the paper:

children.heading: 4 Taxonomy of LLM-Based Credit Risk Assessment

content.text: The papers collected in this section are classified around four main categories: model architectures, data formats, interpretability mechanisms and application areas, and answers are sought to RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, and RQ4.

Recent research on LLM-based credit risk has spanned a variety of domains, from transformer-based architectures to hybrid pipelines and domain-specific fine-tuning to efficient learning. This subsection surveys model architectures for credit risk prediction found in the literature to answer RQ1. Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Model Architectures (RQ1) ‣ 4 Taxonomy of LLM-Based Credit Risk Assessment ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") shows a taxonomy of these models.

* • Encoder-Only Architectures: Encoder-only models (RoBERTa, DistilBERT, FinBERT) are widely used in textual analysis-based financial classification [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. The BERT model derives credit risk indicators and is used to integrate them with tree-based learners [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. FinBERT is reported to perform well in financial sentiment prediction [[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib63)] and fine-tuning in encoder-based benchmarking [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)]. Luca studies the BERT model for credit union use in member transactions [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib38)]. It is also reported that BERT performs robust sentiment extraction in multilingual complex environments [[83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib83)]. * • Decoder-Only Architectures: Decoding models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and ChatGPT) are widely used in generative tasks. Loukas et al. [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)] showed the performance of these models (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) in financial intent classification with a small number of examples (8-20). Similarly, Babaei and Giudici [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib34), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib64)] report the success of GPT in low-data credit scoring scenarios. ChatGPT has been tested by applying it to multidimensional prediction models (financial ratios, social media sentiment) [[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib66)]. Its psychological feature extraction capability is investigated and demonstrated in the GPT-LGBM framework [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib82)]. However, Gupta et al. [[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib69)] mention limitations such as following instructions in complex documents for long-context environments in their study using GPT-4-Turbo. * • Hybrid and Augmented Pipelines: Some frameworks are seen to combine transform-based language modeling with traditional ML models/retrieval mechanisms. In [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)], BERT and GPT are seen to be used together with XGBoost. Another work introduces a structured request pipeline in financial disclosures [[30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib30)]. RAG architectures have gained attention for low-context financial data tasks (news sentiment classification) [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35), [87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib87)]. All these approaches aim to improve the response base by integrating external information sources. * • Domain-Specific Financial LLMs (FinLLMs): Models such as FinGPT, FinMA, ZiGong and FinLLaMA have been built to address domain variations in financial texts. FinGPT is a low-cost framework based on LoRA and Stock Price Reinforcement Learning [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib57)]. Another study initiates the Open FinLLM Leaderboard when comparing financial LLMs and contributes to this field [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib54)]. FinMA framework outperforms GPT-4 on credit-related tasks [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib59)]. ZiGong [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib55)] aims to reduce hallucinations with TracSeq using instruction tuning and temporal pruning methods. FinLMEval emphasizes that the fine-tuning ability of encoder models is superior to the zero-shot power of decoder models in data-scarce environments [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)]. The Open-FinLLMs package supports textual, tabular and visual financial inputs for representing advances in multimodal credit modelling [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib62)]. * • Parameter-Efficient LLMs and Training Techniques: To reduce the computational cost of large models, recent studies have emphasized parameter-efficient methods. Kalluri [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib53)] proposed a study that improves the interaction accuracy and compatibility rates with a scalable solution. In another study, Ni et al. [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib71)] proposes QLoRA-based tuning with LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct-4bit compact models. It is emphasized that the results are better than GPT-4 for gain data. * • Benchmarking and Evaluation Tools: Many recent studies also aim to standardize LLM evaluation in finance. Examples include FinLLM Leaderboard [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib54)], which allows for repeatable testing of financial benchmarks, FinLMEval [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)], which provides analysis of encoder and decoder performance for fine-tuning and zero-shotting. In another study, Lakkaraju et al. [[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib56)] emphasize the concept of fairness for bias models for ChatGPT and Bard outputs.

Recent developments have also witnessed major improvements in the data processed for LLM-focused credit risk assessment. While traditional credit modeling was done with structured tabular data, various data modalities have now emerged, such as unstructured financial text, time series behaviors, multimodal data pipelines, and integration of synthetic data. * • Structured Data: Structured data such as income level and defaults are frequently used in credit scoring studies. GPT-LGBM aims to improve classification performance using this data and ChatGPT [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib82)]. Similarly, PIXIU’s FLARE benchmark and Open-FinLLMs pre-training body use structured data such as technical indicators and historical prices [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib59), [62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib62)]. * • Unstructured Financial Text: Recent studies have reported that unstructured data such as credit disclosures and regulatory documents are important in capturing hidden credit indicators. [[29](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib29)] built enhanced models with free-text disclosures and news sentiment. In other studies, Wu et al. [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib50)] and Sideras et al. [[51](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib51)] examined the impact of manager and auditor comments on default accuracy. [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib55)] filter out low quality sequences in the ZiGong model with a pruning strategy and show the importance of user activity data (time series). Another study integrates psychological features extracted from texts with financial variables in GPT-LGBM [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib82)]. Another hybrid input example is the study by Zhang et al. [[87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib87)] where LLMs are used to enrich external information by combining context-deficient financial text. * • Synthetic and Augmented Data: Factors affecting model performance such as data incompleteness and class imbalances can be addressed using synthetic data-generated LLM models. FinGPT is used to simulate credit records [[31](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib31)], another example is domain-adaptive LLM models trained on SEC filings and Reuters headlines [[39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib39)]. Similarly, Feng et al. [[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib43)] proposed benchmark models for fraud and bankruptcy-related datasets, and the results show success in cross-modality learning.

[[43](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib43)] proposed benchmark models for fraud and bankruptcy-related datasets, and the results show success in cross-modality learning.

Interpretability is an important concept in LLM-based credit risk assessment due to its fairness and reliability. Recent studies aim to increase transparency with methods such as post-hoc methods, internal model designs, instruction setting and model checking strategies. Figure [5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S4.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 4.3 Interpretability Mechanisms (RQ3) ‣ 4 Taxonomy of LLM-Based Credit Risk Assessment ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") shows the taxonomy of interpretability mechanisms.

* • Post-Hoc Explainability: The most commonly used post-hoc methods in this method are SHAP and LIME. Govindaraj et al. [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib32)] proposed a study to visualize local global feature contributions by applying SHAP and attention heatmaps. Liu et al. [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36)] conducted a study combining SHAP and LIME outputs with ChatGPT to make them human interpretable.In [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib50)], LIME’s efficiency in credit assessments is examined, while in [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib67)] SHAP is used with TabTransformer for class skew compensation and interpretability. * • Chain-of-Thought and Prompt- Level Explanations: Recent work aims to enable models to generate explanations directly in the inference pipeline. Dolphin et al. [[30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib30)] use chain-of-thought prompts to provide interpretability in sentiment classification scenarios, while in [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)] they use backoff to improve prediction fixation and tractability. Fatemi et al. [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib52)] show that interpretability can be increased by improving the model’s internal reasoning through instruction tuning. * • Intrinsically Interpretable Model Designs: Some studies propose transparent architectures to reduce the dependency on external explainability tools. One of these models is Logit Leaf, which integrates LLM outputs and segmentation trees, as proposed by Idbenjra et al. [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib47)]. Another study introduces FinBERT-XRC, which can interpret risks at the word and sentence level [[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib46)] . Li et al. To increase model robustness and address hallucinations, in [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib55)], the authors propose a model called TracSeq. [[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib69)] emphasize the importance of F1 score and confidence intervals (CI) metrics for explainability checks. Additionally, Lin et al. [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib54)] advocate benchmarking with the FinLLM Leaderboard to standardize interpretability assessment. * • Ethical, Regulatory, and Theoretical Dimensions: For reliable interpretability, ethics should also be taken into account. Yan et al. Although significant advances have been made in LLM-based financial applications (credit risk estimation, etc.), there are still research gaps and limitations that need to be investigated. Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5 Research Gaps and Future Directions (RQ5) ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") illustrates these limitations.

* • Interpretability Gaps: LLMs applied in finance generally remain black boxes because they rely on post hoc methods (such as SHAP and attention maps) for explainability [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib32), [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36)]. Causal or counterfactual reasoning is almost absent in LLMs applied in finance, and therefore it is difficult to understand the real decision mechanism of the model. Although recent studies ([[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib40)]) propose counterfactual reasoning, its adoption remains minimal. Furthermore, although research is ongoing on LLMs being able to perform automatic classification ([[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib61)]), they are still not widely used in taxonomy studies. * • Reproducibility and Robustness Limitations: Few literature studies have performed robustness testing. Most experiments appear to use small or parsimonious datasets [[33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib33), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)]. Xie et al. [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib59)] reported that FinMA struggles with reasoning tasks and that models trained with human-like instructions are vulnerable. * • Bias, Fairness, and Hallucination Risks: The literature reports that LLMs are prone to bias against demographic characteristics such as race, gender, and age [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36), [56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib56)]. This paper presents the first systematic review and taxonomy of Large Language Model (LLM) based credit risk assessment approaches. The most relevant 60 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 are analyzed using the PRISMA methodology and a structured taxonomy is presented along four main dimensions: model architectures, data formats, interpretability mechanisms, and application domains. The findings confirm that although only coding and domain-specific FinLLMs are frequently used in this field, recent trends in hybrid pipelines, parameter-efficient tuning (e.g. QLoRA), and multimodal data integration are also used in credit scoring. Although SHAP and LIMA (post-hoc) are prevalent interpretability techniques, there is increasing interest in intrinsic and demand-based explanations. Apart from all these developments, there is still a need for further research in the areas of reproducibility, fairness control, robustness to hallucinations, and standardized assessment. We hope that this systematic review and taxonomy study will be a reference paper for researchers in transparent, reliable and field-compatible LLM-based financial risk modeling.

heading_path: Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy
Abstract
chunks.text:
###### Abstract

Large Language Models (LLM), which have developed in recent years, enable credit risk assessment through the analysis of financial texts such as analyst reports and corporate disclosures. This paper presents the first systematic review and taxonomy focusing on LLM-based approaches in credit risk estimation. We determined the basic model architectures by selecting 60 relevant papers published between 2020-2025 with the PRISMA research strategy. And we examined the data used for scenarios such as credit default prediction and risk analysis. Since the main focus of the paper is interpretability, we classify concepts such as explainability mechanisms, chain of thought prompts and natural language justifications for LLM-based credit models.

The taxonomy organizes the literature under four main headings: model architectures, data types, explainability mechanisms and application areas. Based on this analysis, we highlight the main future trends and research gaps for LLM-based credit scoring systems. This paper aims to be a reference paper for artificial intelligence and financial researchers.

This manuscript remains under review.

1 Introduction
chunks.text:
## 1 Introduction

Credit risk assessment is one of the important components in financial decision making, such as making investment decisions and determining whether to grant credit to an individual or institution [[1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib1)]. While traditional methods rely on structured data such as financial ratios and past payment information when assessing credit risk, in reality important information about the credit may not be available in an organized manner [[2](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib2)]. An example of this is that executive comments, economic news and analyst reports are generally in free text (unstructured).

Advanced LLM models such as GPT and FinBERT have great potential in financial applications with their high performance in extracting meaning from free text [[3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib3), [4](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib4)]. They can produce interpretable outputs by making sense of complex financial data and thus facilitate decision-making processes [[5](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib5)]. With its high potential, this research area, LLM-Driven Credit Risk Assessment, where Natural Language Processing (NLP), financial analysis and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) intersect, has begun to attract the attention of researchers. However, the applications of LLMs in the field of credit risk analysis have not yet been systematically examined. The majority of studies in the literature superficially examine the applications of artificial intelligence in the financial sector or do not address the interpretability of LLMs in credit risk assessment in detail. Moreover, this particular research area requires a comprehensive taxonomy of LLM model types, data sources and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques.

## 2 Related Surveys

Although there has been increasing interest in LLM and artificial intelligence (AI)-based financial studies in recent years, there is still no comprehensive classification in terms of focus, depth and relevance to credit risk, and discussions about interpretability, a key component in credit assessment scenarios, are lacking.

Staegemann et al. [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib6)], in their literature review on generative AI applications in banking, highlight the potential of LLMs for risk reduction and customer experience. However, the article does not include techniques for credit risk modeling or interpretability, and there is no taxonomy of model types. In [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib7)], models such as FinGPT and BloombergGPT are discussed, LLMs address financial inclusion and policy implications, and ethical concerns, but ignore credit risk applications. In Joshi et al. study’s AI frameworks in credit risk and trading applications are examined, but does not include LLM architectures or datasets. [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib8)]. Chen et al. [[9](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib9)], in their study of LLMs in finance, law, and healthcare, also highlight the risks of using LLMs in high-risk sectors. However, the financial discussion is superficial, and credit scoring methods are not addressed. In [[10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib10)], sentiment analysis techniques used in banking are reviewed, and the focus is on examining the impact on investor confidence. However, credit risk tasks are only superficially examined. In Nie et al. study’s the research on generative AI and LLMs focused on risk modeling and deployment architectures [[11](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib11)]. The paper discusses areas such as data engineering, credit scoring modules, etc. but lacks a comparative taxonomy and interpretability mechanisms for LLM types. Zavitsanos et al. [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib12)] examines ML approaches in financial risk detection, examining features, data labels, evaluation techniques, and ML methods. Although this is a useful taxonomy, it is more focused on ML than LLM. In [[13](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib13)], the authors mainly emphasize traditional ML and statistical-based methods for financial forecasting, but do not address large language models or explainable AI methods. In Joshi et al. study’s research on AI frameworks in credit risk and trading applications, but does not focus on LLM-specific taxonomy or performance benchmarking [[14](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib14)]. Kong et al. [[15](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib15)] presented a study that benchmarked LLM-based financial tasks for three different languages (Chinese, Japanese, English). However, the model types are not classified and also the explainability is not analyzed for credit risk domains. In Joshi et al. study’s [[16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib16)]. provides detailed architectural review on LLM-based applications for credit scoring and macroeconomic simulations. However, the paper lacks empirical comparison and also lacks a classification for interpretability. Lee et al. [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib17)] review domain-specific financial applications based on LLM, but categorizes flow tasks and datasets, but does not focus on credit risk subdomains. In [[18](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib18)] investigates AI-based methods in financial scenarios such as fraud detection and portfolio management, but does not provide a detailed review of model interpretability and LLM for credit scoring. In Karami and Igbokwe study examines AI-based risk assessment and limitations of traditional credit methods, but does not provide a classification of LLM [[19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib19)]. Alonso et al. [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib20)] provides an overview of LLMs in areas such as asset management and risk reporting, but is insufficient for credit risk. In [[21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib21)], LLMs are studied for financial applications such as credit analysis and fraud detection. However, they are very superficial in interpretability and credit-specific modeling. Lakkaraju et al. [[22](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib22)] evaluates LLM performance through a fairness lens, focuses on bias reduction strategies such as improving user trust, but credit risk assessments and explainability are very superficial. In [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib23)], LLM-based financial sentiment analysis with multiple datasets is not considered credit risk or XAI. Omoseebi et al. [[24](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib24)] investigates the financial security side of LLMs such as fraud detection, but does not perform detailed credit risk modeling and taxonomy studies. In [[25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib25)], democratization of financial datasets and open data models of LLMs are discussed, but no empirical comparison is included for credit or risk analytics. Krause et al. [[26](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib26)] present a survey discussing the sustainability of LLM models such as ChatGPT. The survey is mostly on ethical and governance concerns and is superficial in terms of credit scoring, model breakdowns, and datasets. In [[27](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib27)], the robustness of LLMs in financial tasks is assessed and benchmarks are made on summarization and event detection. However, the study does not include credit-related tasks and explainability is weak.

Comparison of Surveys: Table [1](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2 Related Surveys ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") provides a comparison of the surveys examined in this section. While interest in the financial domain applications of LLMs is increasing day by day, existing studies focus on broad themes such as generative AI [[6](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib6)], inclusiveness frameworks [[7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib7)] and financial NLP [[17](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib17), [21](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib21)]. Only a limited number of studies directly focus on credit risk tasks, and none of them provide a taxonomy by examining LLM architectures, data formats, interpretability techniques and domain-specific applications.

Furthermore, most studies do not provide interpretability for high-risk decisions such as credit scoring, and the studies that do provide interpretability are very superficial [[20](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib20), [25](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib25)]. Some of the surveys include studies such as sentiment analysis or fraud detection [[23](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib23), [10](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib10)], but they do not address the concept of credit risk modeling. Some of the reviewed studies focus only on traditional machine learning (ML) [[12](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib12), [19](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib19)] and only propose conceptual frameworks without model comparison [[8](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib8), [16](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib16)].

Although some of the studies discuss domain-specific LLMs (such as FinBERT, FinGPT, and InvestLM), they do not systematically model architecture or risk. None of the existing studies provide a classification of LLM applications that addresses both modeling and regulatory requirements (e.g., explainability, data provenance, or fairness). This study is the first to fill this gap based on four main pillars: model architecture, data modality, interpretability mechanism, and application domain.

### 4.1 Model Architectures (RQ1)

Recent research on LLM-based credit risk has spanned a variety of domains, from transformer-based architectures to hybrid pipelines and domain-specific fine-tuning to efficient learning. This subsection surveys model architectures for credit risk prediction found in the literature to answer RQ1. Figure [3](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.1 Model Architectures (RQ1) ‣ 4 Taxonomy of LLM-Based Credit Risk Assessment ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") shows a taxonomy of these models.

* • Encoder-Only Architectures: Encoder-only models (RoBERTa, DistilBERT, FinBERT) are widely used in textual analysis-based financial classification [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. The BERT model derives credit risk indicators and is used to integrate them with tree-based learners [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. FinBERT is reported to perform well in financial sentiment prediction [[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib63)] and fine-tuning in encoder-based benchmarking [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)]. Luca studies the BERT model for credit union use in member transactions [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib38)]. It is also reported that BERT performs robust sentiment extraction in multilingual complex environments [[83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib83)]. * • Decoder-Only Architectures: Decoding models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and ChatGPT) are widely used in generative tasks. Loukas et al. [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)] showed the performance of these models (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) in financial intent classification with a small number of examples (8-20). Similarly, Babaei and Giudici [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib34), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib64)] report the success of GPT in low-data credit scoring scenarios. ChatGPT has been tested by applying it to multidimensional prediction models (financial ratios, social media sentiment) [[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib66)]. Its psychological feature extraction capability is investigated and demonstrated in the GPT-LGBM framework [[82](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib82)]. However, Gupta et al. [[69](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib69)] mention limitations such as following instructions in complex documents for long-context environments in their study using GPT-4-Turbo. * • Hybrid and Augmented Pipelines: Some frameworks are seen to combine transform-based language modeling with traditional ML models/retrieval mechanisms. In [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)], BERT and GPT are seen to be used together with XGBoost. Another work introduces a structured request pipeline in financial disclosures [[30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib30)]. RAG architectures have gained attention for low-context financial data tasks (news sentiment classification) [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35), [87](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib87)]. All these approaches aim to improve the response base by integrating external information sources. * • Domain-Specific Financial LLMs (FinLLMs): Models such as FinGPT, FinMA, ZiGong and FinLLaMA have been built to address domain variations in financial texts. FinGPT is a low-cost framework based on LoRA and Stock Price Reinforcement Learning [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib57)]. Another study initiates the Open FinLLM Leaderboard when comparing financial LLMs and contributes to this field [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib54)]. FinMA framework outperforms GPT-4 on credit-related tasks [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib59)]. ZiGong [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib55)] aims to reduce hallucinations with TracSeq using instruction tuning and temporal pruning methods. FinLMEval emphasizes that the fine-tuning ability of encoder models is superior to the zero-shot power of decoder models in data-scarce environments [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)]. The Open-FinLLMs package supports textual, tabular and visual financial inputs for representing advances in multimodal credit modelling [[62](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib62)]. * • Parameter-Efficient LLMs and Training Techniques: To reduce the computational cost of large models, recent studies have emphasized parameter-efficient methods. Kalluri [[53](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib53)] proposed a study that improves the interaction accuracy and compatibility rates with a scalable solution. In another study, Ni et al. [[71](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib71)] proposes QLoRA-based tuning with LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct-4bit compact models. It is emphasized that the results are better than GPT-4 for gain data. * • Benchmarking and Evaluation Tools: Many recent studies also aim to standardize LLM evaluation in finance. Examples include FinLLM Leaderboard [[54](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib54)], which allows for repeatable testing of financial benchmarks, FinLMEval [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)], which provides analysis of encoder and decoder performance for fine-tuning and zero-shotting. In another study, Lakkaraju et al. [[56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib56)] emphasize the concept of fairness for bias models for ChatGPT and Bard outputs.

Encoder-Only Architectures: Encoder-only models (RoBERTa, DistilBERT, FinBERT) are widely used in textual analysis-based financial classification [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. The BERT model derives credit risk indicators and is used to integrate them with tree-based learners [[28](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib28)]. FinBERT is reported to perform well in financial sentiment prediction [[63](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib63)] and fine-tuning in encoder-based benchmarking [[85](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib85)]. Luca studies the BERT model for credit union use in member transactions [[38](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib38)]. It is also reported that BERT performs robust sentiment extraction in multilingual complex environments [[83](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib83)].

Decoder-Only Architectures: Decoding models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and ChatGPT) are widely used in generative tasks. Loukas et al. [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)] showed the performance of these models (GPT-3.5 and GPT-4) in financial intent classification with a small number of examples (8-20). Similarly, Babaei and Giudici [[34](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib34), [64](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib64)] report the success of GPT in low-data credit scoring scenarios.

ChatGPT has been tested by applying it to multidimensional prediction models (financial ratios, social media sentiment) [[66](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib66)]. ### 4.3 Interpretability Mechanisms (RQ3)

Interpretability is an important concept in LLM-based credit risk assessment due to its fairness and reliability. Recent studies aim to increase transparency with methods such as post-hoc methods, internal model designs, instruction setting and model checking strategies. * • Post-Hoc Explainability: The most commonly used post-hoc methods in this method are SHAP and LIME. Govindaraj et al. [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib32)] proposed a study to visualize local global feature contributions by applying SHAP and attention heatmaps. Liu et al. [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36)] conducted a study combining SHAP and LIME outputs with ChatGPT to make them human interpretable.In [[50](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib50)], LIME’s efficiency in credit assessments is examined, while in [[67](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib67)] SHAP is used with TabTransformer for class skew compensation and interpretability. * • Chain-of-Thought and Prompt- Level Explanations: Recent work aims to enable models to generate explanations directly in the inference pipeline. Dolphin et al. [[30](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib30)] use chain-of-thought prompts to provide interpretability in sentiment classification scenarios, while in [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)] they use backoff to improve prediction fixation and tractability. Fatemi et al. [[52](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib52)] show that interpretability can be increased by improving the model’s internal reasoning through instruction tuning. * • Intrinsically Interpretable Model Designs: Some studies propose transparent architectures to reduce the dependency on external explainability tools. One of these models is Logit Leaf, which integrates LLM outputs and segmentation trees, as proposed by Idbenjra et al. [[47](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib47)]. Another study introduces FinBERT-XRC, which can interpret risks at the word and sentence level [[46](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib46)] . Li et al. To increase model robustness and address hallucinations, in [[55](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib55)], the authors propose a model called TracSeq. In another study, the authors aim to improve interpretability by combining gain deltas and the QLoRA model. * • Fairness, Auditing, and Reproducibility: Other concepts that are directly related to interpretability are fairness and reproducibility. [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib68)] examine the performance of GPT/BERT-based models on AML, sanctions screening, and suspicious activity.

Investment, Trading, and Asset Management: Walia et al. [[45](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib45)] apply LLMs to bond yield prediction and extend the use of LLMs in finance. [[57](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib57)] evaluate the performance of FinGPT in robo-advisory and algorithmic trading bots. ## 5 Research Gaps and Future Directions (RQ5)

Although significant advances have been made in LLM-based financial applications (credit risk estimation, etc.), there are still research gaps and limitations that need to be investigated. Figure [7](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5 Research Gaps and Future Directions (RQ5) ‣ Interpretable LLMs for Credit Risk: A Systematic Review and Taxonomy") illustrates these limitations.

* • Interpretability Gaps: LLMs applied in finance generally remain black boxes because they rely on post hoc methods (such as SHAP and attention maps) for explainability [[32](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib32), [36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36)]. Causal or counterfactual reasoning is almost absent in LLMs applied in finance, and therefore it is difficult to understand the real decision mechanism of the model. Although recent studies ([[40](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib40)]) propose counterfactual reasoning, its adoption remains minimal. Furthermore, although research is ongoing on LLMs being able to perform automatic classification ([[61](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib61)]), they are still not widely used in taxonomy studies. * • Reproducibility and Robustness Limitations: Few literature studies have performed robustness testing. Most experiments appear to use small or parsimonious datasets [[33](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib33), [35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35)]. Xie et al. [[59](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib59)] reported that FinMA struggles with reasoning tasks and that models trained with human-like instructions are vulnerable. * • Bias, Fairness, and Hallucination Risks: The literature reports that LLMs are prone to bias against demographic characteristics such as race, gender, and age [[36](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib36), [56](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib56)]. Furthermore, LLMs can produce false information, hallucinations, that are very close to the truth, and these remain a major threat to credit risk estimation [[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib37)]. Few frameworks in the literature target fairness and hallucination reduction [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib68)]. * • Efficiency and Model Scaling: Very few of the studies consider metrics such as latency, inference cost, and hardware performance [[35](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib35), [39](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib39)]. Furthermore, LLMs can produce false information, hallucinations, that are very close to the truth, and these remain a major threat to credit risk estimation [[37](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib37)]. Few frameworks in the literature target fairness and hallucination reduction [[68](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/2506.04290#bib.bib68)].

## 6 Conclusions

This paper presents the first systematic review and taxonomy of Large Language Model (LLM) based credit risk assessment approaches. The most relevant 60 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2025 are analyzed using the PRISMA methodology and a structured taxonomy is presented along four main dimensions: model architectures, data formats, interpretability mechanisms, and application domains. The findings confirm that although only coding and domain-specific FinLLMs are frequently used in this field, recent trends in hybrid pipelines, parameter-efficient tuning (e.g. QLoRA), and multimodal data integration are also used in credit scoring. Although SHAP and LIMA (post-hoc) are prevalent interpretability techniques, there is increasing interest in intrinsic and demand-based explanations. Apart from all these developments, there is still a need for further research in the areas of reproducibility, fairness control, robustness to hallucinations, and standardized assessment. We hope that this systematic review and taxonomy study will be a reference paper for researchers in transparent, reliable and field-compatible LLM-based financial risk modeling.
